title: Ὕπνου ὅρκος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Aphrodite has given Hera the strap, and Hera smiles and tucks it into her bosom. She goes from Olympus over Pieria, Emathia and the Thracian mountains, by way of Athos to Lemnos, and there takes Sleep by the hand and asks him to close Zeus’s eyes once she has lain with him, promising a golden throne made by Hephaestus. Sleep refuses: he can put any other god to sleep, even Oceanus, but Zeus only if Zeus himself bids him, and once before, when Heracles sailed from Troy, he lulled Zeus at Hera’s command and Zeus nearly hurled him into the sea, until Night saved him. Hera answers by offering one of the younger Graces as his wife; Sleep asks for an oath by the Styx, naming Pasithea, and Hera swears it, calling on the Titans. The two go through the mist to Ida, where Sleep climbs a tall fir and sits hidden in it like a bird. Hera climbs Gargarus, and Zeus, seeing her, is overcome with desire. She tells him she is on her way to settle the quarrel of Oceanus and Tethys, and Zeus answers that she can go later and asks her to lie down with him, saying that no woman or goddess he ever loved, neither Ixion’s wife, Danae, the daughter of Phoenix, Semele, Alcmene, Demeter nor Leto, nor Hera herself, ever stirred him as she does now.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη,
μειδήσασα δ’ ἔπειτα ἑῷ ἐγκάτθετο κόλπῳ.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, meidēsen de boōpis potnia Hērē,
meidēsasa d’ epeita heōi enkattheto kolpōi.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and smiled ox-eyed lady Hera,
and smiling then she laid it up in her own bosom.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and ox-eyed lady Hera smiled, and with a smile tucked it into her own bosom.
sentences.n: Aphrodite has just finished speaking (the last unit of the previous part ends her speech), and ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ closes it with φάτο, the unaugmented past of φημί. βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη is Hera’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way. ‘It’ is the embroidered strap Aphrodite gave her. ἑῷ is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative, and ἐγκάτθετο is the aorist middle of ἐγκατατίθημι ‘lay up in’, with its preposition shortened; the same verb in the imperative was the order near the end of the last part.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἔβη πρὸς δῶμα Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη,
Ἥρη δ’ ἀΐξασα λίπεν ῥίον Οὐλύμποιο,
sentences.tr:
hē men ebē pros dōma Dios thygatēr Aphroditē,
Hērē d’ aïxasa lipen rhion Oulympoio,
sentences.l:
She, for her part, went to the house, Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite,
and Hera, darting, left the crag of Olympus,
sentences.i: Aphrodite, Zeus’s daughter, went off to the house, and Hera darted off and left the crag of Olympus,
sentences.n: ἣ μέν … Ἥρη δέ sets the two goddesses side by side: ‘she, for her part … but Hera’. Διὸς θυγάτηρ is ‘daughter of Zeus’, and ἀΐξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’, used of a swift start. ῥίον is a jutting height, a crag or peak. The sentence runs on to the ano teleia in line 228, so it is cut here at a comma.

sentences.t:
Πιερίην δ’ ἐπιβᾶσα καὶ Ἠμαθίην ἐρατεινὴν
σεύατ’ ἐφ’ ἱπποπόλων Θρῃκῶν ὄρεα νιφόεντα
ἀκροτάτας κορυφάς·
sentences.tr:
Pieriēn d’ epibasa kai Ēmathiēn erateinēn
seuat’ eph’ hippopolōn Thrēikōn orea niphoenta
akrotatas koryphas·
sentences.i: stepping on Pieria and lovely Emathia, she rushed over the snowy mountains of the horse-herding Thracians, to their topmost peaks;
sentences.n: ἐπιβᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘set foot on’, here with the names of two regions in the accusative. σεύατ’ is σεύατο, the aorist middle of σεύω ‘rush’, unaugmented. ἐφ’ … ὄρεα is ‘to/over the mountains’, and ἀκροτάτας κορυφάς, ‘the topmost peaks’, stands in apposition to them. ἱπποπόλων ‘horse-herding’ is a stock epithet of the Thracians, translated every time in the same way. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 228.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ χθόνα μάρπτε ποδοῖιν·
sentences.tr: oude chthona marpte podoiin·
sentences.l: and she did not touch the ground with her feet;
sentences.i: and she did not touch the ground with her feet;
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia. μάρπτε is an imperfect without augment (Attic ἔμαρπτε), ‘was touching’, from μάρπτω ‘seize, lay hold of’. ποδοῖιν is a dual dative, ‘with her two feet’, in the old ending -οῖιν. She travels above the ground.

sentences.t:
ἐξ Ἀθόω δ’ ἐπὶ πόντον ἐβήσετο κυμαίνοντα,
Λῆμνον δ’ εἰσαφίκανε πόλιν θείοιο Θόαντος.
sentences.tr:
ex Athoō d’ epi ponton ebēseto kymainonta,
Lēmnon d’ eisaphikane polin theioio Thoantos.
sentences.l:
and from Athos onto the swelling sea she went,
and she came to Lemnos, the city of divine Thoas.
sentences.i: and from Athos she went out over the swelling sea, and came to Lemnos, the city of divine Thoas.
sentences.n: ἐξ Ἀθόω is ‘from Athos’, the genitive of the mountain’s name in the epic ending -όω. ἐβήσετο is the aorist middle of βαίνω with σ, ‘went, set out’, and κυμαίνοντα is ‘swelling, rising in waves’, a participle of κυμαίνω agreeing with πόντον. εἰσαφίκανε is the imperfect of εἰσαφικάνω ‘arrive at’, unaugmented. Λῆμνον … πόλιν is ‘the city Lemnos’, with θείοιο Θόαντος ‘of divine Thoas’ (θείοιο is the epic genitive of θεῖος ‘divine’).

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ὕπνῳ ξύμβλητο κασιγνήτῳ Θανάτοιο,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Hypnōi xymblēto kasignētōi Thanatoio,
en t’ ara hoi phy cheiri epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l:
There she met Sleep, brother of Death,
and she clasped him by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: There she met Sleep, brother of Death, and took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ξύμβλητο is an aorist middle of συμβάλλω ‘meet’ with the epic ξυν- for συν-, no augment, and it takes the dative Ὕπνῳ. Ὕπνος ‘Sleep’ and Θάνατος ‘Death’ are persons here. ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί is literally ‘she grew into his hand’, that is, clung to it (φῦ is the aorist of φύω, unaugmented, with ἐν in tmesis), and ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the stock phrase ‘spoke a word and called by name’ (ἐκ … ὀνόμαζεν is tmesis), translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
Ὕπνε ἄναξ πάντων τε θεῶν πάντων τ’ ἀνθρώπων,
ἠμὲν δή ποτ’ ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες, ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν
πείθευ·
sentences.tr:
Hypne anax pantōn te theōn pantōn t’ anthrōpōn,
ēmen dē pot’ emon epos eklyes, ēd’ eti kai nyn
peitheu·
sentences.i: “Sleep, lord of all the gods and of all men, as you once listened to my word, so now too obey me;
sentences.n: The speech is Hera’s, and the Greek has no quotation marks. Ὕπνε ἄναξ is address, ‘Sleep, lord’, with the genitives πάντων … θεῶν and πάντων … ἀνθρώπων (τε … τε ‘both … and’). ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is the epic ‘both … and’, and here has the sense ‘as … so’: ἔκλυες is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear, listen to’, and πείθευ is the present imperative middle of πείθω, ‘obey’ (with the dative understood, ‘me’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 235.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι ἰδέω χάριν ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.tr: egō de ke toi ideō charin ēmata panta.
sentences.l: and I shall know gratitude to you all my days.
sentences.i: and I shall be grateful to you all my days.
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. ἰδέω is a subjunctive of οἶδα ‘know’ (Attic εἰδῶ), with κε giving it the force of a future: χάριν εἰδέναι ‘to know thanks’ is the Greek idiom for ‘to be grateful’. τοι is ‘to you’, and ἤματα πάντα is the accusative of duration, ‘all the days’.

sentences.t:
κοίμησόν μοι Ζηνὸς ὑπ’ ὀφρύσιν ὄσσε φαεινὼ
αὐτίκ’ ἐπεί κεν ἐγὼ παραλέξομαι ἐν φιλότητι.
sentences.tr:
koimēson moi Zēnos hyp’ ophrysin osse phaeinō
autik’ epei ken egō paralexomai en philotēti.
sentences.l:
Put to sleep for me beneath his brows the two shining eyes of Zeus
at once, as soon as I shall have lain beside him in love.
sentences.i: Put the shining eyes of Zeus to sleep for me beneath his brows, at once, as soon as I have lain down beside him in love.
sentences.n: κοίμησον is the aorist imperative of κοιμάω ‘put to sleep’, with μοι ‘for me’ and ὄσσε φαεινώ, a dual, ‘the two shining eyes’ (ὄσσε is a dual noun, ‘the eyes’). ὑπ’ ὀφρύσιν is ‘beneath the brows’, and ὀφρύσιν is the dative plural of ὀφρῦς. ἐπεί κεν with παραλέξομαι (a form that can be read as a future or as a short-vowel aorist subjunctive) ‘when I shall have lain beside’ is the Greek way to say ‘as soon as’; αὐτίκ’ ‘at once’ can go with the command or with the clause. ἐν φιλότητι is ‘in love’, the word for sexual love here, as it will be again in 314.

sentences.t:
δῶρα δέ τοι δώσω καλὸν θρόνον ἄφθιτον αἰεὶ
χρύσεον·
sentences.tr:
dōra de toi dōsō kalon thronon aphthiton aiei
chryseon·
sentences.l:
And gifts I shall give you: a fair throne, imperishable for ever,
golden;
sentences.i: And I shall give you gifts: a fair throne, golden and imperishable for ever;
sentences.n: δῶρα ‘gifts’ is the general word, and καλὸν θρόνον ἄφθιτον … χρύσεον ‘a fair throne, imperishable, golden’ names the gift. ἄφθιτον ‘imperishable’ is from ἀ- and φθίνω ‘waste away, perish’, and αἰεί ‘for ever’ is the epic form of ἀεί. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 239.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστος δέ κ’ ἐμὸς πάϊς ἀμφιγυήεις
τεύξει’ ἀσκήσας, ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυν ποσὶν ἥσει,
τῷ κεν ἐπισχοίης λιπαροὺς πόδας εἰλαπινάζων.
sentences.tr:
Hēphaistos de k’ emos païs amphigyēeis
teuxei’ askēsas, hypo de thrēnyn posin hēsei,
tōi ken epischoiēs liparous podas eilapinazōn.
sentences.l:
and Hephaestus, my son, the both-limbed one,
would make it, working it with skill, and beneath it for the feet he will set a footstool,
on which you could rest your sleek feet, feasting.”
sentences.i: and Hephaestus, my son, the both-limbed god, would make it, working it with skill, and set a footstool beneath it for your feet, on which you could rest your sleek feet as you feasted.”
sentences.n: ἀμφιγυήεις ‘both-limbed’ is Hephaestus’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way; its meaning is not known, and ‘both-limbed’ (from ἀμφί and γυῖον ‘limb’) is only the traditional reading. τεύξει’ is the optative τεύξειε of τεύχω ‘make’, with κ’ (κε) as a potential, ‘would make’; ἀσκήσας is ‘having worked it with skill’ (ἀσκέω). ἥσει is the future of ἵημι, with ὑπό in tmesis (ὑπὸ … ἥσει = ὑφήσει), ‘will put under’, and θρῆνυν is its object. τῷ is ‘on this’, the footstool (θρῆνυς is masculine), and ἐπισχοίης is a potential optative, ‘you could rest’. λιπαροὺς πόδας εἰλαπινάζων ‘sleek feet, feasting’ is close to a phrase the Odyssey also has (λιπαροὺς πόδας εἰλαπινάζων, 17.410). This is the end of Hera’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε νήδυμος Ὕπνος·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephōnee nēdymos Hypnos·
sentences.l: To her answering spoke sweet Sleep:
sentences.i: In answer sweet Sleep spoke to her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε is a speech-introduction: τὴν ‘her’ is the pronoun-article, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, and προσεφώνεε the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. νήδυμος ‘sweet’ is Sleep’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way; its meaning and origin are not known, and ‘sweet’ is traditional.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη πρέσβα θεὰ θύγατερ μεγάλοιο Κρόνοιο
ἄλλον μέν κεν ἔγωγε θεῶν αἰειγενετάων
ῥεῖα κατευνήσαιμι, καὶ ἂν ποταμοῖο ῥέεθρα
Ὠκεανοῦ, ὅς περ γένεσις πάντεσσι τέτυκται·
sentences.tr:
Hērē presba thea thygater megaloio Kronoio
allon men ken egōge theōn aieigenetaōn
rheia kateunēsaimi, kai an potamoio rheethra
Ōkeanou, hos per genesis pantessi tetyktai·
sentences.l:
“Hera, august goddess, daughter of great Cronus,
another, of the gods who are forever-born, I could
easily put to sleep, and even the streams of the river
Oceanus, who has been made the origin for all;
sentences.i: “Hera, august goddess, daughter of great Cronus, any other of the everlasting gods I could easily put to sleep, and even the streams of the river Oceanus, who is the origin of all;
sentences.n: The first line is the same address as the one Hera was given at 14.194. ἄλλον μέν is ‘another, for one’, set against Ζηνὸς δέ in the next unit; θεῶν αἰειγενετάων is ‘of the forever-born gods’, with the epic genitive plural in -άων (αἰειγενέτης is masculine). κατευνήσαιμι is a potential optative of κατευνάω ‘put to sleep’, and καὶ ἂν … ῥέεθρα means ‘even the streams’, with the modal ἂν repeated for the second object. ὅς περ γένεσις πάντεσσι τέτυκται is ‘who has become the origin for all’ (τέτυκται is the perfect of τεύχω, ‘has been made, is’, and πάντεσσι is the epic dative plural).

sentences.t:
Ζηνὸς δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγε Κρονίονος ἆσσον ἱκοίμην
οὐδὲ κατευνήσαιμ’, ὅτε μὴ αὐτός γε κελεύοι.
sentences.tr:
Zēnos d’ ouk an egōge Kronionos asson hikoimēn
oude kateunēsaim’, hote mē autos ge keleuoi.
sentences.l:
But of Zeus, the son of Cronus, I could not come nearer,
nor put him to sleep, unless he himself should bid me.
sentences.i: But I could not come near Zeus, the son of Cronus, or put him to sleep, unless he himself should bid me.
sentences.n: Ζηνός is the genitive of Ζεύς, and ἆσσον ἱκοίμην ‘come nearer to’ takes it; οὐκ ἂν … ἱκοίμην and οὐδὲ κατευνήσαιμ’ are potential optatives, ‘I could not come near … nor put to sleep’. Κρονίονος is the epic genitive of Κρονίων, ‘son of Cronus’. ὅτε μή is ‘except when, unless’, with κελεύοι, the optative, giving a condition set in the unlikely future (‘should he bid’).

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ με καὶ ἄλλο τεὴ ἐπίνυσσεν ἐφετμὴ
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε κεῖνος ὑπέρθυμος Διὸς υἱὸς
ἔπλεεν Ἰλιόθεν Τρώων πόλιν ἐξαλαπάξας.
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar me kai allo teē epinyssen ephetmē
ēmati tōi hote keinos hyperthymos Dios huios
epleen Iliothen Trōōn polin exalapaxas.
sentences.l:
For already at another time too your command goaded me,
on that day when that high-spirited son of Zeus
was sailing from Ilios, having sacked the city of the Trojans.
sentences.i: For on another occasion, too, your command already goaded me, on the day when that high-spirited son of Zeus sailed from Ilios, having sacked the city of the Trojans.
sentences.n: ἐπίνυσσεν is the imperfect of ἐπινύσσω, which is literally ‘prick, goad’; how it applies to a ‘command’ (ἐφετμή) is not known for certain, and ‘goaded me’ is the traditional rendering, the command that drove Sleep into trouble, as the following lines show. καὶ ἄλλο is ‘at another time, too’, and με is ‘me’. ὑπέρθυμος ‘high-spirited’ is a stock epithet. Διὸς υἱός is not named here: the son is Heracles, whom Hera names in 266. ἔπλεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of πλέω, ‘was sailing’, and Ἰλιόθεν is ‘from Ilios’ (the suffix -θεν marks ‘from’). ἐξαλαπάξας is the aorist participle of ἐξαλαπάζω ‘sack’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἐγὼ μὲν ἔλεξα Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο
νήδυμος ἀμφιχυθείς·
sentences.tr:
ētoi egō men elexa Dios noon aigiochoio
nēdymos amphichytheis·
sentences.l:
Indeed I, for my part, put to sleep the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus,
pouring myself around him, sweet;
sentences.i: I, for my part, lulled the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus, pouring myself around him, sweet;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ‘indeed’ (the edition prints it as one word) and ἐγὼ μέν set Sleep’s part against Hera’s in the next unit (σὺ δέ). ἔλεξα is an aorist of λέγω in its old sense ‘lay down’, so ‘put to rest, lulled’. Διὸς νόον is ‘the mind of Zeus’, and αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way; its meaning is disputed. ἀμφιχυθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀμφιχέω ‘pour round’, which describes sleep as a liquid spreading over him. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 253.

sentences.t:
σὺ δέ οἱ κακὰ μήσαο θυμῷ
ὄρσασ’ ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων ἐπὶ πόντον ἀήτας,
καί μιν ἔπειτα Κόων δ’ εὖ ναιομένην ἀπένεικας
νόσφι φίλων πάντων.
sentences.tr:
sy de hoi kaka mēsao thymōi
orsas’ argaleōn anemōn epi ponton aētas,
kai min epeita Koōn d’ eu naiomenēn apeneikas
nosphi philōn pantōn.
sentences.l:
but you evil things for him devised in your heart,
having stirred up over the sea the blasts of grievous winds,
and him then to well-inhabited Cos you carried away
away from all his dear ones.
sentences.i: but you devised evil for him in your heart: you stirred up the blasts of grievous winds over the sea, and then carried him off to well-inhabited Cos, away from all his dear ones.
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. σύ δέ οἱ κακὰ μήσαο is ‘but you devised evils for him’ (μήσαο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘plan’, and οἱ is ‘for him’, the epic dative), and ὄρσασ’ is the aorist participle of ὄρνυμι, ‘having stirred up’. ἀργαλέων ‘grievous’ goes with ἀνέμων ἀήτας ‘blasts of winds’. Κόων δ’ is the accusative Κόων (of Κῶς) with the suffix -δε elided, ‘to Cos’, and εὖ ναιομένην is ‘well inhabited’, a participle of ναίω agreeing with it. μιν is Heracles (see 249–251), and ἀπένεικας is the aorist of ἀποφέρω. The unit ends at a full stop in mid-line 256.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπεγρόμενος χαλέπαινε
ῥιπτάζων κατὰ δῶμα θεούς, ἐμὲ δ’ ἔξοχα πάντων
ζήτει·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epegromenos chalepaine
rhiptazōn kata dōma theous, eme d’ exocha pantōn
zētei·
sentences.i: But he, when he woke, was furiously angry, flinging the gods about the house, and sought me out beyond all others;
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. ὁ δέ is ‘but he’, Zeus (the pronoun-article), and ἐπεγρόμενος is the aorist participle middle of ἐπεγείρω, ‘having woken’, with χαλέπαινε, an imperfect of χαλεπαίνω without its augment (χαλεπός ‘harsh’, read as a mood of anger: ‘was growing harsh’). ῥιπτάζων is ‘flinging’ (the frequentative of ῥίπτω), with the gods as object and κατὰ δῶμα ‘about the house’; ἔξοχα πάντων is ‘beyond all others’. ζήτει is the imperfect of ζητέω, unaugmented, ‘was seeking’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 258.

sentences.t:
καί κέ μ’ ἄϊστον ἀπ’ αἰθέρος ἔμβαλε πόντῳ,
εἰ μὴ Νὺξ δμήτειρα θεῶν ἐσάωσε καὶ ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr:
kai ke m’ aïston ap’ aitheros embale pontōi,
ei mē Nyx dmēteira theōn esaōse kai andrōn·
sentences.l:
and he would have thrown me, unseen, out of the aether into the sea,
if Night, tamer of gods and of men, had not saved me;
sentences.i: and he would have flung me, vanished from sight, from the upper air into the sea, if Night, who tames gods and men, had not saved me;
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. καί κε … ἔμβαλε is an unreal past with κε and an unaugmented ‘he would have thrown’ (ἔμβαλε = ἐνέβαλε), and εἰ μὴ … ἐσάωσε is ‘if … had not saved’. ἄϊστον is ‘unseen, gone from sight’ (ἀ- and the root of ἰδεῖν ‘see’), and αἰθέρος is ‘the aether’ in the sense of the bright upper air, against ἠέρος ‘the mist’ below. Νὺξ δμήτειρα is ‘Night, the tamer’ (δμήτειρα is from δαμάζω ‘subdue’), with the genitives θεῶν καὶ ἀνδρῶν.

sentences.t: τὴν ἱκόμην φεύγων, ὃ δ’ ἐπαύσατο χωόμενός περ.
sentences.tr: tēn hikomēn pheugōn, ho d’ epausato chōomenos per.
sentences.l: to her I came, fleeing, and he stopped, though angry.
sentences.i: I came to her in my flight, and he stopped, angry though he was.
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, Night (ἱκόμην is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, with the accusative), and φεύγων is ‘fleeing’. ὁ δέ is Zeus again, ἐπαύσατο ‘stopped’ the aorist middle of παύω, and χωόμενός περ is ‘though angry’ (χώομαι ‘be angry’; περ is ‘even though’).

sentences.t: ἅζετο γὰρ μὴ Νυκτὶ θοῇ ἀποθύμια ἕρδοι.
sentences.tr: hazeto gar mē Nykti thoēi apothymia herdoi.
sentences.l: For he was in awe lest he do things unwelcome to swift Night.
sentences.i: For he shrank from doing anything to displease swift Night.
sentences.n: ἅζετο is the imperfect of ἅζομαι ‘be in awe of, shrink from’, and μὴ … ἕρδοι is ‘lest he do’ (an optative after a past tense, with ἕρδω ‘do’). ἀποθύμια is ‘things unwelcome, displeasing’ (ἀπό and θυμός ‘heart’). Νυκτὶ θοῇ is ‘swift Night’, in the dative with ἀποθύμια.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖ τοῦτό μ’ ἄνωγας ἀμήχανον ἄλλο τελέσσαι.
sentences.tr: nyn au touto m’ anōgas amēchanon allo telessai.
sentences.l: Now again this other thing past help you bid me accomplish.”
sentences.i: And now you bid me accomplish this other thing, which is past all remedy.”
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ is ‘now again’, and τοῦτο … ἄλλο ἀμήχανον is ‘this other thing past help’ (ἀμήχανον ‘without resource, past help’ is from ἀ- and μηχανή ‘means’), the object of ἄνωγας ‘you bid’ with the infinitive τελέσσαι (aorist of τελέω ‘accomplish’, doubled σ for the verse). This is the end of Sleep’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe boōpis potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is a stock reply-line, with αὖτε ‘in turn, again’ and προσέειπε ‘addressed’ (the epic form of προσεῖπε; its augment is the first ε). The speaker is Hera, with her stock epithet βοῶπις πότνια ‘ox-eyed lady’.

sentences.t: Ὕπνε τί ἢ δὲ σὺ ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς;
sentences.tr: Hypne ti ē de sy tauta meta phresi sēisi menoināis;
sentences.l: “Sleep, why do you these things in your wits have in mind?
sentences.i: “Sleep, why do you have these things in your mind?
sentences.n: τί is ‘why’, and ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς is ‘you have these things in your wits’ (μενοινάω ‘have in mind, intend, yearn for’; μετά with the dative, ‘among’, here ‘in’; σῇσι is ‘your’, the epic dative plural of σός). The edition prints τί ἢ δέ here (for the usual τίη δέ); the particles sharpen the question (‘why, then’) and are left unrendered. φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν.

sentences.t:
ἦ φῂς ὣς Τρώεσσιν ἀρηξέμεν εὐρύοπα Ζῆν
ὡς Ἡρακλῆος περιχώσατο παῖδος ἑοῖο;
sentences.tr:
ē phēis hōs Trōessin arēxemen euryopa Zēn
hōs Hēraklēos perichōsato paidos heoio;
sentences.l:
Do you say, really, that so to the Trojans will give aid far-thundering Zeus,
as he was greatly angry for Heracles, his own son?
sentences.i: Do you really say that far-thundering Zeus will help the Trojans just as he was angered over Heracles, his own son?
sentences.n: ἦ is the particle that opens a yes-or-no question, and φῂς is ‘you say’ (φημί, second person singular). The Greek has ὣς … ὡς, ‘so … as’: Zeus will help the Trojans in the way he was angry over Heracles. ἀρηξέμεν is the epic future infinitive of ἀρήγω ‘help’ (= ἀρήξειν), and Ζῆν is the accusative of Ζεύς. εὐρύοπα ‘far-thundering’ is a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way. περιχώσατο is the aorist middle of περιχώομαι ‘be very angry for the sake of’, with the genitive Ἡρακλῆος, and ἑοῖο is ‘his own’, the possessive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθ’, ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι Χαρίτων μίαν ὁπλοτεράων
δώσω ὀπυιέμεναι καὶ σὴν κεκλῆσθαι ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ ith’, egō de ke toi Charitōn mian hoploteraōn
dōsō opuiemenai kai sēn keklēsthai akoitin.
sentences.l:
But go: and I shall give you one of the younger Graces
to marry and to be called your wife.”
sentences.i: But go: I shall give you one of the younger Graces to marry and to be called your wife.”
sentences.n: ἴθ’ is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’, and Χαρίτων μίαν ὁπλοτεράων is ‘one of the younger Graces’ (ὁπλοτεράων is the epic genitive plural of ὁπλότερος ‘younger’). δώσω with the infinitives ὀπυιέμεναι (ὀπυίω ‘take as wife’, the epic -έμεναι) and κεκλῆσθαι (the perfect passive infinitive of καλέω ‘be called’) is ‘I shall give … to marry and to be called’. σήν is ‘your’, the ordinary possessive σός. This is the end of Hera’s speech. The edition’s numbering skips from 268 to 270.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, χήρατο δ’ Ὕπνος, ἀμειβόμενος δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, chērato d’ Hypnos, ameibomenos de prosēuda·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and Sleep rejoiced, and answering he spoke to her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Sleep was glad, and said to her in answer:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the usual ‘so she spoke’. χήρατο is the aorist middle of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, in the epic form with the augment dropped, and ἀμειβόμενος … προσηύδα is ‘answering, he spoke to her’ (προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω). The edition numbers this line 270; there is no line 269.

sentences.t: ἄγρει νῦν μοι ὄμοσσον ἀάατον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ,
sentences.tr: agrei nyn moi omosson aaaton Stygos hydōr,
sentences.l: “Come now, swear to me the inviolable water of the Styx,
sentences.i: “Come now, swear to me by the inviolable water of the Styx,
sentences.n: ἄγρει νῦν is ‘come now’, and ὄμοσσον is the aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’ (the doubled σ is the epic form), here with the accusative of the thing sworn by: Στυγὸς ὕδωρ ‘the water of the Styx’, the gods’ dread oath. ἀάατον is of uncertain meaning, and ‘inviolable’ (not to be harmed, from ἀ- and ἀάω ‘harm’) is the traditional gloss, not a certainty.

sentences.t:
χειρὶ δὲ τῇ ἑτέρῃ μὲν ἕλε χθόνα πουλυβότειραν,
τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ ἅλα μαρμαρέην, ἵνα νῶϊν ἅπαντες
μάρτυροι ὦσ’ οἳ ἔνερθε θεοὶ Κρόνον ἀμφὶς ἐόντες,
sentences.tr:
cheiri de tēi heterēi men hele chthona poulyboteiran,
tēi d’ heterēi hala marmareēn, hina nōïn hapantes
martyroi ōs’ hoi enerthe theoi Kronon amphis eontes,
sentences.l:
and with the one hand take hold of the much-nourishing earth,
and with the other the gleaming sea, so that for us two all
may be witnesses, the gods below, who are around Cronus,
sentences.i: and take hold of the earth that feeds so many with one hand and the gleaming sea with the other, so that all the gods below, those who are around Cronus, may be witnesses for the two of us,
sentences.n: ἕλε is the aorist imperative of αἱρέω, ‘take’, and μὲν … δέ sets χειρὶ τῇ ἑτέρῃ ‘with the one hand’ against τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ ‘with the other’. πουλυβότειραν is ‘nourishing many’, from βόσκω ‘feed’, and the house rendering is ‘much-nourishing’ in the first layer and ‘that feeds so many’ in the second; μαρμαρέην is ‘gleaming’. νῶϊν is a dual dative, ‘for us two’. ἵνα … ὦσ’ is ‘so that … may be’ (ὦσι, the subjunctive of εἰμί), with μάρτυροι ‘witnesses’, and οἳ ἔνερθε θεοί is ‘the gods below’. ἀμφὶς ἐόντες Κρόνον is ‘being around Cronus’ (ἐόντες is the epic participle of εἰμί).

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν ἐμοὶ δώσειν Χαρίτων μίαν ὁπλοτεράων
Πασιθέην, ἧς τ’ αὐτὸς ἐέλδομαι ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.tr:
ē men emoi dōsein Charitōn mian hoploteraōn
Pasitheēn, hēs t’ autos eeldomai ēmata panta.
sentences.l:
that truly to me you will give one of the younger Graces,
Pasithea, for whom I myself long all my days.”
sentences.i: that you will truly give me one of the younger Graces, Pasithea, for whom I myself long all my days.”
sentences.n: ἦ μέν ‘truly’ introduces the content of the oath, which the infinitive δώσειν ‘you will give’ carries (the subject, ‘you’, is understood). Πασιθέην ‘Pasithea’ is named as the Grace; ἧς τ’ αὐτὸς ἐέλδομαι is ‘for whom I myself long’ (ἐέλδομαι ‘long for’ takes the genitive, and ἧς is the relative). This is the end of Sleep’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
ὄμνυε δ’ ὡς ἐκέλευε, θεοὺς δ’ ὀνόμηνεν ἅπαντας
τοὺς ὑποταρταρίους οἳ Τιτῆνες καλέονται.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse thea leukōlenos Hērē,
omnye d’ hōs ekeleue, theous d’ onomēnen hapantas
tous hypotartarious hoi Titēnes kaleontai.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
and she swore as he bade, and named the gods, all of them,
those beneath Tartarus, who are called Titans.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, did not disobey; she swore as he bade, and named all the gods beneath Tartarus, who are called Titans.
sentences.n: The first line is a stock formula; λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is Hera’s epithet, translated every time in the same way. ὄμνυε is the imperfect of ὄμνυμι, unaugmented, and ὡς ἐκέλευε is ‘as he bade’. ὀνόμηνεν is the aorist of ὀνομαίνω ‘name’, and τοὺς ὑποταρταρίους is ‘those beneath Tartarus’ (ὑπό and Τάρταρος), with the relative οἳ … καλέονται ‘who are called’, the uncontracted καλέονται. Τιτῆνες is ‘Titans’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσέν τε τελεύτησέν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
τὼ βήτην Λήμνου τε καὶ Ἴμβρου ἄστυ λιπόντε
ἠέρα ἑσσαμένω ῥίμφα πρήσσοντε κέλευθον.
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ omosen te teleutēsen te ton horkon,
tō bētēn Lēmnou te kai Imbrou asty liponte
ēera hessamenō rhimpha prēssonte keleuthon.
sentences.l:
But when then she had sworn and finished the oath,
the two went, Lemnos’ and Imbros’ town leaving,
clothed in mist, nimbly making their way.
sentences.i: And when she had sworn and completed the oath, the two of them set out, leaving the town of Lemnos and Imbros, clothed in mist, nimbly making their way.
sentences.n: The first line is a stock line: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσέν τε τελεύτησέν τε τὸν ὅρκον ‘but when she had sworn and completed the oath’. τὼ βήτην is ‘the two went’, with duals throughout: βήτην (the dual of ἔβησαν), λιπόντε ‘having left’, ἑσσαμένω ‘having clothed themselves’ (the aorist middle of ἕννυμι) and πρήσσοντε ‘accomplishing’. Λήμνου τε καὶ Ἴμβρου ἄστυ is ‘the town of Lemnos and of Imbros’. ἠέρα ‘mist’ is the lower air, and ῥίμφα is ‘nimbly’. πρήσσοντε κέλευθον is ‘making their way’ (literally ‘accomplishing the road’).

sentences.t:
Ἴδην δ’ ἱκέσθην πολυπίδακα μητέρα θηρῶν
Λεκτόν, ὅθι πρῶτον λιπέτην ἅλα·
sentences.tr:
Idēn d’ hikesthēn polypidaka mētera thērōn
Lekton, hothi prōton lipetēn hala·
sentences.l:
And to Ida they came, many-springed, mother of wild beasts,
to Lectum, where first they left the sea;
sentences.i: and they came to Ida of many springs, mother of wild beasts, to Lectum, where they first left the sea;
sentences.n: ἱκέσθην and λιπέτην are duals, ‘the two came’ and ‘the two left’ (ἱκέσθην is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι; λιπέτην is the aorist of λείπω, unaugmented). πολυπίδακα is ‘many-springed’, a stock epithet of Ida, translated every time in the same way, and μητέρα θηρῶν ‘mother of wild beasts’ is the other. Λεκτόν is the place where they reach land after crossing the sea, and ὅθι ‘where’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 284.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου
βήτην, ἀκροτάτη δὲ ποδῶν ὕπο σείετο ὕλη.
sentences.tr:
tō d’ epi chersou
bētēn, akrotatē de podōn hypo seieto hylē.
sentences.l:
and the two over dry land
went, and the topmost woodland shook beneath their feet.
sentences.i: and the two went on over dry land, and the topmost woods shook under their feet.
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. τὼ δ’ is ‘and the two’, and ἐπὶ χέρσου ‘over dry land’ takes the genitive. ἀκροτάτη … ὕλη is ‘the topmost woodland’, and ποδῶν ὕπο is ‘beneath their feet’, with the preposition after its noun. σείετο is the imperfect passive of σείω, ‘was shaken, shook’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ὕπνος μὲν ἔμεινε πάρος Διὸς ὄσσε ἰδέσθαι
εἰς ἐλάτην ἀναβὰς περιμήκετον, ἣ τότ’ ἐν Ἴδῃ
μακροτάτη πεφυυῖα δι’ ἠέρος αἰθέρ’ ἵκανεν·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Hypnos men emeine paros Dios osse idesthai
eis elatēn anabas perimēketon, hē tot’ en Idēi
makrotatē pephyuia di’ ēeros aither’ hikanen·
sentences.i: There Sleep stopped, before he should look on the eyes of Zeus, having climbed into a very tall fir, which then, as the tallest tree that grew on Ida, reached up through the mist to the upper air;
sentences.n: ἔμεινε is ‘stayed, waited’, and πάρος … ἰδέσθαι is ‘before looking at’: ἰδέσθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἰδεῖν, with Διὸς ὄσσε ‘the eyes of Zeus’ as its object, so Sleep halts short of Zeus’s sight. ἀναβάς is the aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω ‘climb’, and ἐλάτην … περιμήκετον is ‘a very tall fir’. μακροτάτη is the superlative of μακρός, ‘tallest’, and πεφυυῖα is the perfect participle of φύω ‘grow’. ἠέρος is the lower air or mist, the aether the upper air; the tree’s top reaches through the one into the other.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἧστ’ ὄζοισιν πεπυκασμένος εἰλατίνοισιν
ὄρνιθι λιγυρῇ ἐναλίγκιος, ἥν τ’ ἐν ὄρεσσι
χαλκίδα κικλήσκουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δὲ κύμινδιν.
sentences.tr:
enth’ hēst’ ozoisin pepykasmenos eilatinoisin
ornithi ligyrēi enalinkios, hēn t’ en oressi
chalkida kiklēskousi theoi, andres de kymindin.
sentences.l:
There he sat, thickly covered with fir boughs,
like a clear-sounding bird, which in the mountains
the gods call chalkis, and men kymindis.
sentences.i: There he sat, hidden among the fir boughs, like a clear-sounding bird, which in the mountains the gods call chalkis, and men kymindis.
sentences.n: ἧστ’ is ἧστο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ὄζοισιν … εἰλατίνοισιν is ‘with fir boughs’ (the dative plural -οισιν, with εἰλατίνοισιν for ἐλατίνοισιν, ‘of fir’). πεπυκασμένος is the perfect passive participle of πυκάζω, ‘thickly covered, screened’. ἐναλίγκιος is ‘like’, with the dative, and λιγυρῇ ‘clear-sounding’ describes the bird’s voice. The bird has two names, one used by the gods and one by men: χαλκίδα and κύμινδιν are both accusative, after κικλήσκουσι ‘call’. The bird is not identified here.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δὲ κραιπνῶς προσεβήσετο Γάργαρον ἄκρον
Ἴδης ὑψηλῆς·
sentences.tr:
Hērē de kraipnōs prosebēseto Gargaron akron
Idēs hypsēlēs·
sentences.l:
And Hera at a rush went up to Gargarus, the peak
of lofty Ida;
sentences.i: And Hera at a rush climbed to Gargarus, the peak of lofty Ida;
sentences.n: προσεβήσετο is the aorist middle of προσβαίνω, ‘went up to’, with the same -σετο form as in 229. κραιπνῶς is ‘at a rush’, and Γάργαρον ἄκρον ‘Gargarus, the peak’ names the highest point of Ἴδης ὑψηλῆς ‘lofty Ida’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 293.

sentences.t: ἴδε δὲ νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς.
sentences.tr: ide de nephelēgereta Zeus.
sentences.l: and cloud-gatherer Zeus saw her.
sentences.i: and Zeus who gathers the clouds saw her.
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. ἴδε is ἴδε(ν) ‘saw’, unaugmented (= εἶδε), and has no object expressed, ‘her’ being understood from the sentence before. νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is the stock epithet and name, with the epic nominative in -α, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ἴδεν, ὥς μιν ἔρως πυκινὰς φρένας ἀμφεκάλυψεν,
οἷον ὅτε πρῶτόν περ ἐμισγέσθην φιλότητι
εἰς εὐνὴν φοιτῶντε, φίλους λήθοντε τοκῆας.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ iden, hōs min erōs pykinas phrenas amphekalypsen,
hoion hote prōton per emisgesthēn philotēti
eis eunēn phoitōnte, philous lēthonte tokēas.
sentences.l:
And as he saw her, so desire covered his close-packed wits all around,
such as when first they mingled in love,
going to bed, escaping the notice of their dear parents.
sentences.i: And as soon as he saw her, desire covered his close-packed mind all around, as when they first lay together in love, going to bed in secret from their dear parents.
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ἴδεν, ὥς μιν … ἀμφεκάλυψεν is ‘as he saw, so it covered him’; ἴδεν is unaugmented, ἔρως ‘desire’ is the subject, and πυκινὰς φρένας ‘close-packed wits’ the object, with ἀμφεκάλυψεν the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘cover round’. οἷον ὅτε πρῶτόν περ is ‘as when first’. ἐμισγέσθην, φοιτῶντε and λήθοντε are duals, ‘the two mingled, going, escaping the notice of’, and λήθοντε takes the accusative φίλους τοκῆας ‘their dear parents’. εἰς εὐνήν is ‘to bed’.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ αὐτῆς προπάροιθεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ autēs proparoithen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l: He stood before her, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: He stood in front of her, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, and αὐτῆς προπάροιθεν is ‘before her herself’, with the genitive. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the stock phrase, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t: Ἥρη πῇ μεμαυῖα κατ’ Οὐλύμπου τόδ’ ἱκάνεις;
sentences.tr: Hērē pēi memauia kat’ Oulympou tod’ hikaneis;
sentences.l: “Hera, where eager from Olympus down do you come to this place?
sentences.i: “Hera, where are you so eager to go, that you come down here from Olympus?
sentences.n: πῇ ‘where’ with μεμαυῖα, the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, is ‘where, eager (to go)?’. κατ’ Οὐλύμπου is ‘down from Olympus’ (κατά with the genitive), and τόδ’ ἱκάνεις ‘you come to this place’ (ἱκάνω ‘come to’ takes the accusative). The speech has no quotation marks in the Greek.

sentences.t: ἵπποι δ’ οὐ παρέασι καὶ ἅρματα τῶν κ’ ἐπιβαίης.
sentences.tr: hippoi d’ ou pareasi kai harmata tōn k’ epibaiēs.
sentences.l: and your horses are not here, nor the chariots, those you could mount.”
sentences.i: Your horses are not here, nor the chariots that you could mount.”
sentences.n: παρέασι is the epic παρεῖσι, ‘are present’ (ἔασι = εἰσί). ἵπποι and ἅρματα ‘horses’ and ‘chariots’ are the subjects, and τῶν κ’ ἐπιβαίης is ‘of which you might mount’ (ἐπιβαίνω takes the genitive, and the optative with κε is potential). This is the end of Zeus’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ δολοφρονέουσα προσηύδα πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: ton de dolophroneousa prosēuda potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: And to him, with guile in her mind, spoke lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then lady Hera, with guile in her mind, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ δολοφρονέουσα προσηύδα πότνια Ἥρη is a speech-introduction: δολοφρονέουσα ‘with guile in her mind’ (the participle of δολοφρονέω, from δόλος ‘guile’ and φρήν), and προσηύδα ‘spoke to’. πότνια Ἥρη ‘lady Hera’ is the stock epithet and name. What follows is a lie, since Hera has another purpose than the one she gives.

sentences.t:
ἔρχομαι ὀψομένη πολυφόρβου πείρατα γαίης,
Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν,
οἵ με σφοῖσι δόμοισιν ἐῢ τρέφον ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλον·
sentences.tr:
erchomai opsomenē polyphorbou peirata gaiēs,
Ōkeanon te theōn genesin kai mētera Tēthyn,
hoi me sphoisi domoisin eÿ trephon ēd’ atitallon·
sentences.i: “I am going to see the ends of the much-nourishing earth, and Oceanus, the origin of the gods, and mother Tethys, who reared me well in their own house and fostered me;
sentences.n: ἔρχομαι ὀψομένη is ‘I am going, to see’ (ὀψομένη is the future participle of ὁράω, expressing purpose), and πείρατα is ‘ends, limits’. The second line is the same as 14.201 in the last part: Ὠκεανόν … γένεσιν and μητέρα Τηθύν. οἵ is the relative, ‘who’ (Oceanus and Tethys), and σφοῖσι δόμοισιν is ‘in their own houses’ (σφοῖσι is the possessive ‘their own’). ἐῢ τρέφον ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλον is ‘reared well and fostered’, two unaugmented imperfects (τρέφω; ἀτιτάλλω ‘foster’).

sentences.t: τοὺς εἶμ’ ὀψομένη, καί σφ’ ἄκριτα νείκεα λύσω·
sentences.tr: tous eim’ opsomenē, kai sph’ akrita neikea lysō·
sentences.l: them I am going to see, and their unsorted quarrels I shall loose;
sentences.i: I am going to see them, and I shall settle their endless quarrels;
sentences.n: τοὺς εἶμ’ ὀψομένη is ‘them I am going to see’ (εἶμι ‘I am going’ with the future participle of purpose), and τοὺς refers to Oceanus and Tethys. σφ’ is the enclitic third-person plural pronoun, here best given as ‘their’, and ἄκριτα νείκεα is ‘unsorted quarrels’, quarrels with no judgment on them, from ἀ- and κρίνω; λύσω is ‘I shall loose, settle’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ δηρὸν χρόνον ἀλλήλων ἀπέχονται
εὐνῆς καὶ φιλότητος, ἐπεὶ χόλος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar dēron chronon allēlōn apechontai
eunēs kai philotētos, epei cholos empese thymōi.
sentences.l:
for already for a long time from one another they have kept away,
from bed and from love, since anger fell upon their heart.
sentences.i: For they have already been keeping away from one another for a long time, from bed and from love, since anger fell upon their hearts.
sentences.n: ἤδη … δηρὸν χρόνον is ‘already for a long time’, and ἀπέχονται is the present middle of ἀπέχω with the genitive ‘keep away from’: ἀλλήλων ‘from one another’, εὐνῆς καὶ φιλότητος ‘from bed and from love’. ἔμπεσε is the unaugmented aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’, with χόλος ‘anger’ as subject and θυμῷ as ‘heart’ in the singular, though two people are meant. Hera uses the gods’ separation as her cover.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δ’ ἐν πρυμνωρείῃ πολυπίδακος Ἴδης
ἑστᾶσ’, οἵ μ’ οἴσουσιν ἐπὶ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν.
sentences.tr:
hippoi d’ en prymnōreiēi polypidakos Idēs
hestas’, hoi m’ oisousin epi trapherēn te kai hygrēn.
sentences.l:
And the horses at the foot of many-springed Ida
stand, which will carry me over the solid land and the wet.
sentences.i: The horses are standing at the foot of Ida of many springs, and they will carry me over land and sea.
sentences.n: ἐν πρυμνωρείῃ is ‘at the foot of the mountain’, with the epic dative in -ῃ, and πολυπίδακος Ἴδης is ‘many-springed Ida’. ἑστᾶσ’ is ἑστᾶσι, the perfect of ἵστημι, ‘stand’. οἵ is the relative ‘which’, and οἴσουσιν is the future of φέρω ‘carry’. τραφερήν and ὑγρήν are feminine adjectives with no noun, ‘the solid (land) and the wet (sea)’, which is a way of saying ‘land and sea’; the second layer gives it so.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ σεῦ εἵνεκα δεῦρο κατ’ Οὐλύμπου τόδ’ ἱκάνω,
μή πώς μοι μετέπειτα χολώσεαι, αἴ κε σιωπῇ
οἴχωμαι πρὸς δῶμα βαθυρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.tr:
nyn de seu heineka deuro kat’ Oulympou tod’ hikanō,
mē pōs moi metepeita cholōseai, ai ke siōpēi
oichōmai pros dōma bathyrroou Ōkeanoio.
sentences.l:
But now for your sake here from Olympus down I have come to this place,
lest in some way afterwards you be angry with me, if in silence
I should go off to the house of deep-flowing Oceanus.”
sentences.i: But now I have come down here from Olympus for your sake, so that you will not be angry with me afterwards, if I should go off in silence to the house of deep-flowing Oceanus.”
sentences.n: σεῦ εἵνεκα is ‘for your sake’ (σεῦ is the epic genitive of σύ, and εἵνεκα = ἕνεκα), and δεῦρο … τόδ’ ἱκάνω repeats the words of Zeus’s question in 298. μή πώς … χολώσεαι is ‘lest in some way you be angry’ (χολώσεαι is the second person singular middle of χολόω, in the epic -εαι, and can be read as a future or as a short-vowel aorist subjunctive after μή), and αἴ κε … οἴχωμαι is ‘if ever I should go off’ (αἴ κε is εἰ κε ‘if’, with the subjunctive), with σιωπῇ ‘in silence’. βαθυρρόου ‘deep-flowing’ is a stock epithet of Oceanus, translated every time in the same way. This is the end of Hera’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: The line is a stock reply-formula, with τὴν ‘her’ and ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’. νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is the stock epithet and name, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη κεῖσε μὲν ἔστι καὶ ὕστερον ὁρμηθῆναι,
νῶϊ δ’ ἄγ’ ἐν φιλότητι τραπείομεν εὐνηθέντε.
sentences.tr:
Hērē keise men esti kai hysteron hormēthēnai,
nōï d’ ag’ en philotēti trapeiomen eunēthente.
sentences.l:
“Hera, thither it is possible to set out later too,
but we two, come, let us turn to love, having lain down.
sentences.i: “Hera, you can go there later too; but come, let the two of us turn to love, lying down together.
sentences.n: κεῖσε is ‘thither’, and ἔστι … ὁρμηθῆναι is ‘it is possible to set out’ (ὁρμηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ὁρμάω). νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, and ἄγ’ is ‘come’. ἐν φιλότητι τραπείομεν is ‘let us turn to love’ (τραπείομεν is the epic aorist passive subjunctive of τρέπω, first person plural, ‘let us turn’). εὐνηθέντε is a dual participle, ‘the two having lain down’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ ποτέ μ’ ὧδε θεᾶς ἔρος οὐδὲ γυναικὸς
θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι περιπροχυθεὶς ἐδάμασσεν,
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō pote m’ hōde theas eros oude gynaikos
thymon eni stēthessi periprochytheis edamassen,
sentences.l:
For never yet me thus has desire for goddess or woman
my heart in my breast, poured around it, subdued,
sentences.i: For never yet has desire for a goddess or a woman poured itself around the heart in my breast and overpowered me so,
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ … πώ ποτε is ‘for never yet’, and the sentence has an accusative of the person and the part: μ’ … θυμὸν … ἐδάμασσεν is ‘subdued me, my heart’. ἔρος is the epic form of ἔρως ‘desire’, and θεᾶς οὐδὲ γυναικός is ‘for a goddess or a woman’, the genitive of the object. περιπροχυθείς is the aorist passive participle of περιπροχέω, ‘poured round’; ἐδάμασσεν is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘overpower’. The line begins a list of earlier loves that runs to 328, cut here and below at its stops.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὁπότ’ ἠρασάμην Ἰξιονίης ἀλόχοιο,
ἣ τέκε Πειρίθοον θεόφιν μήστωρ’ ἀτάλαντον·
sentences.tr:
oud’ hopot’ ērasamēn Ixioniēs alochoio,
hē teke Peirithoon theophin mēstōr’ atalanton·
sentences.l:
nor when I fell in love with the wife of Ixion,
who bore Peirithous, the gods’ equal, a counsellor;
sentences.i: nor when I fell in love with Ixion’s wife, who bore Peirithous, a counsellor equal to the gods;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὁπότε … ἠρασάμην is ‘nor when I fell in love’ (ἠρασάμην is the aorist of ἔραμαι, which takes the genitive, here Ἰξιονίης ἀλόχοιο ‘Ixion’s wife’; Ἰξιονίης is an adjective, ‘Ixion’s’). ἣ τέκε is ‘who bore’ (unaugmented). θεόφιν is ‘to gods’ (the epic ending -φιν does duty for the dative or genitive), with ἀτάλαντον ‘equal’, and μήστωρ’ is μήστωρα ‘a counsellor’, in apposition to Peirithous. Peirithous is the son of this union.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅτε περ Δανάης καλλισφύρου Ἀκρισιώνης,
ἣ τέκε Περσῆα πάντων ἀριδείκετον ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ hote per Danaēs kallisphyrou Akrisiōnēs,
hē teke Persēa pantōn arideiketon andrōn·
sentences.l:
nor when it was Danae, fair-ankled, daughter of Acrisius,
who bore Perseus, the most conspicuous of all men;
sentences.i: nor when it was Danae, the fair-ankled daughter of Acrisius, who bore Perseus, the most distinguished of all men;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅτε περ is ‘nor even when’, and Δανάης … Ἀκρισιώνης is the genitive ‘of Danae … daughter of Acrisius’, with Ἀκρισιώνη as a patronymic in the feminine. καλλισφύρου is ‘fair-ankled’, translated every time in the same way. ἀριδείκετον is ‘most conspicuous’ (ἀρι- is an intensive prefix and the second part is from the root of δείκνυμι ‘show’), with πάντων … ἀνδρῶν ‘of all men’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅτε Φοίνικος κούρης τηλεκλειτοῖο,
ἣ τέκε μοι Μίνων τε καὶ ἀντίθεον Ῥαδάμανθυν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ hote Phoinikos kourēs tēlekleitoio,
hē teke moi Minōn te kai antitheon Rhadamanthyn·
sentences.l:
nor when it was the daughter of Phoenix, far-famed,
who bore to me Minos and godlike Rhadamanthys;
sentences.i: nor when it was the far-famed daughter of Phoenix, who bore me Minos and godlike Rhadamanthys;
sentences.n: Φοίνικος κούρης is ‘the daughter of Phoenix’, and τηλεκλειτοῖο is ‘far-famed’ (τῆλε ‘far’ and κλειτός ‘famed’), with the epic genitive in -οιο. ἣ τέκε μοι is ‘who bore to me’. ἀντίθεον is ‘godlike’, a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅτε περ Σεμέλης οὐδ’ Ἀλκμήνης ἐνὶ Θήβῃ,
ἥ ῥ’ Ἡρακλῆα κρατερόφρονα γείνατο παῖδα·
sentences.tr:
oud’ hote per Semelēs oud’ Alkmēnēs eni Thēbēi,
hē rh’ Hēraklēa kraterophrona geinato paida·
sentences.l:
nor when it was Semele, nor Alcmene in Thebes,
who bore Heracles, strong-minded, as her son;
sentences.i: nor when it was Semele, nor Alcmene in Thebes, she who bore Heracles of strong mind as her son;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅτε περ … is ‘nor even when’, with Σεμέλης οὐδ’ Ἀλκμήνης ‘of Semele nor of Alcmene’, and ἐνὶ Θήβῃ ‘in Thebes’ (ἐνί is the epic form of ἐν). ἥ ῥ’ … γείνατο is ‘she who bore’, and Alcmene is the mother of Heracles (the next line gives Semele’s son). κρατερόφρονα ‘strong-minded’ is a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way, and παῖδα is ‘as a child’, in apposition.

sentences.t: ἣ δὲ Διώνυσον Σεμέλη τέκε χάρμα βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr: hē de Diōnyson Semelē teke charma brotoisin·
sentences.l: and she, Semele, bore Dionysus, a joy to mortals;
sentences.i: while Semele bore Dionysus, a joy to mortals;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ … Σεμέλη is ‘but she, Semele’, and ἣ δέ picks up the double name of 323. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω ‘bear’. χάρμα βροτοῖσιν is ‘a joy to mortals’ (χάρμα ‘joy’ in apposition to Dionysus, and βροτοῖσιν the dative plural).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅτε Δήμητρος καλλιπλοκάμοιο ἀνάσσης,
οὐδ’ ὁπότε Λητοῦς ἐρικυδέος, οὐδὲ σεῦ αὐτῆς,
ὡς σέο νῦν ἔραμαι καί με γλυκὺς ἵμερος αἱρεῖ.
sentences.tr:
oud’ hote Dēmētros kalliplokamoio anassēs,
oud’ hopote Lētous erikydeos, oude seu autēs,
hōs seo nyn eramai kai me glykys himeros hairei.
sentences.l:
nor when it was Demeter, the fair-plaited queen,
nor when it was Leto, glorious, nor you yourself,
as now I desire you and sweet longing seizes me.”
sentences.i: nor when it was Demeter, the fair-plaited queen, nor glorious Leto, nor you yourself, as I now desire you and sweet longing seizes me.”
sentences.n: Δήμητρος καλλιπλοκάμοιο ἀνάσσης is ‘Demeter, the queen, fair-plaited’ (καλλιπλοκάμοιο ‘fair-plaited’ is the epic genitive in -οιο, and ἀνάσσης is ‘queen’), and Λητοῦς ἐρικυδέος is ‘glorious Leto’. The last item is σεῦ αὐτῆς ‘you yourself’, the epic genitive σεῦ, and the list ends on Hera. ὡς σέο νῦν ἔραμαι is ‘as I now desire you’ (ἔραμαι takes the genitive), and ἵμερος ‘longing’ is the subject of αἱρεῖ ‘seizes’. This is the end of Zeus’s speech.
